title: A tenth
hook: Christian tithes, Muslim zakat, Sikh dasvandh: each tradition sets aside a share

segments.voice: Yesterday, the love of money, and the Buddha's householder told to put his wealth to good use. Your line was put to good use. What did you spend on purpose? Today, the share some traditions set aside before anything else. Day nine hundred sixteen.

A paycheck lands. Before the rent, before the groceries, before anything else, a small piece is moved somewhere else: an envelope in a church, a transfer to a mosque's fund for the poor, a donation box at a gurdwara. For some who give this way, this isn't charity left over at the end of the month, if there's anything left. It's set aside on purpose, sometimes before anything else is paid. Today: a tenth.
screen: `A PAYCHECK LANDS.` → `OFF THE TOP.` → `THE FIRST THING PAID.`

segments.voice: First, the tithe. In Genesis, after a battle, Abram meets Melchizedek, a priest and king, and "he gave him tithes of all." The letter to the Hebrews, looking back on that scene, spells it out: Abraham "gave the tenth of the spoils." Later, the prophet Malachi says, "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house." Some Christians today give a tenth of their income to their church; others see the tenth as a guide rather than a rule, and give in their own measure. Second, zakat. The Qur'an pairs prayer with zakat, a required giving, and it names who should receive it, among them the poor, the needy, those in debt and the traveler. Zakat isn't a tenth of income; Muslim teaching sets it as a share of certain kinds of wealth, and the share differs from one kind to another. But like the tithe, it's not optional generosity. It's an act of worship, and in Muslim teaching it purifies the wealth that remains. Third, dasvandh. In Sikh tradition, dasvandh is the practice of setting aside a tenth of one's earnings for the community and those in need, often given through the gurdwara, where it can help keep the free kitchen running. Fourth, what they share. The amounts and rules differ, and each tradition has its own reasons. But each one sets a share aside on purpose and regularly. That turns giving from a mood into a habit. And each, in its own way, treats part of what comes in as belonging to others.
screen: `THE TITHE: A TENTH OF ALL.` · `ZAKAT: PRAYER'S PARTNER.` · `DASVANDH: A TENTH FOR OTHERS.` · `A SHARE SET ASIDE ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `A TENTH.`

segments.voice: Imagine the share, for these two minutes. Picture the money that comes to you this month, from a paycheck, an allowance, a pension, whatever it is. Now picture setting aside a small piece first, before anything else, and putting it in an envelope marked for others. It doesn't need to be a tenth. Notice what happens in you as you set it aside. Then picture where it might go: a person, a cause, a community. The bell holds the time.
A tenth. The tithe, the Sikh dasvandh, and alongside them the Muslim zakat: a share of what comes in, set aside on purpose for others. Today's word.
Your line: a share for others. Today, set aside a small share of what you have, any amount, and decide where it will go. Day nine hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some Christians tithe a tenth of their income to their church; Muslims calculate and pay zakat each year on qualifying wealth; Sikhs who keep dasvandh set aside a tenth of their earnings, often through the gurdwara.

notes: Qur'an 2:43 (prayer paired with zakat) and 9:60 (recipients) are paraphrased. 'Pairs prayer with zakat' summarizes several verses; a Muslim Keeper should confirm. Zakat's rate and the lunar-year holding period (hawl) are left out under the claims rule, described only as 'a set share of certain kinds of wealth they've held through the year'.
'In Muslim teaching it purifies the wealth that remains' reflects the common understanding of zakat (cf. Qur'an 9:103); confirm framing.

A Sikh Keeper should confirm the description of dasvandh as a tenth of earnings, given for the community and those in need, often through the gurdwara, and confirm the Gurmukhi ਦਸਵੰਧ and pronunciation.
Melchizedek bringing bread and wine (Genesis 14:18) is used in the fork; 'a priest and king' follows the text.
Christian practice: 'some give a tenth; others see it as a guide' is kept deliberately without counts.

Editor: fixed the garbled zakat line ('they've held') and cut the holding-year claim; cut 'before the money can be spent' (not true of zakat) and the narrator's 'never only yours to keep'; dropped the repeated 'if you pray' line; varied practice opener.

Audit (serious): 'zakat isn't figured as a tenth' was wrong as stated (classical zakat on rain-fed crops is a tenth); now 'isn't a tenth of income' and the share differs by kind of wealth. Hook and word no longer say the share always comes 'off the top', which does not fit zakat's yearly reckoning.
